Confidence interval of a survey proportion

Source: R/svyci.R
svypci.Rd

An interval for a proportion estimated from a complex survey, from the estimate and its design-based standard error (those of svymx(), say). The usual interval, the estimate plus and minus a multiple of its standard error (Wald), is too narrow for a small sample or a proportion near 0 or 1, and can leave the range 0 to 1; statistical agencies ask for one of the three others here instead.

Usage

svypci(
  est,
  se,
  n,
  df = n - 1,
  method = c("beta", "wilson", "logit", "wald"),
  level = 0.95,
  trunc = TRUE
)

Arguments

est

The estimated proportion, from 0 to 1.

se

Its standard error.

n

The number of respondents of the sample (unweighted).

df

The degrees of freedom of the design: first-stage units less strata, as svymx() reports; n - 1 by default (a simple random sample).

method

"beta" (the default), "wilson", "logit" or "wald".

level

The confidence level of the intervals.

trunc

TRUE (the default) keeps the effective sample size at or below n.

Value

A data frame with a row per estimate: est, lo, hi and neff, the effective sample size ne* (for every method: it is what the design is worth). NA where an input is missing, and for the logit interval at 0 or 1.

Details

The first two put the design into an effective sample size, the size of a simple random sample with the same variance, ne = p (1 - p) / se^2, corrected for the degrees of freedom of the design (Korn and Graubard 1998): ne* = ne (t(n - 1) / t(df))^2, with t() the quantile of Student's t at the level. With trunc, the default, ne* is never above n, as Korn and Graubard and SAS have it; survey::svyciprop() does not truncate, and trunc = FALSE gives its interval. An estimate of exactly 0 or 1, or a standard error of 0, has no effective size of its own and takes n.

"beta": the Clopper-Pearson interval at ne* with p ne* events, by beta quantiles (Korn and Graubard 1998): the "modified Clopper-Pearson" interval. "wilson": the Wilson score interval at ne* with the normal quantile: the "modified Wilson" interval (Dean and Pagano 2015). "logit": the Wald interval of log(p / (1 - p)), with standard error se / (p (1 - p)) and Student's t on df, taken back to a proportion; it does not exist at 0 or 1. "wald": p plus and minus the t quantile times se, the interval svymx() gives.

Health Canada's guides to the Canadian surveys of alcohol and drug use recommend, in this order, the modified Wilson, the modified Clopper-Pearson and the logit interval, and advise against the Wald interval (Health Canada 2022, section 7.3).

Errors: est outside 0 to 1; se negative; n not a whole number of at least 2; df below 1; level outside (0, 1); method not one of the four; trunc not TRUE or FALSE; arguments that are not numeric or of different lengths (a length of 1 is repeated).

References

Korn, E. L. and Graubard, B. I. (1998). Confidence intervals for proportions with small expected number of positive counts estimated from survey data. Survey Methodology, 24(2), 193-201.

Dean, N. and Pagano, M. (2015). Evaluating confidence interval methods for binomial proportions in clustered surveys. Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology, 3(4), 484-503. doi:10.1093/jssam/smv024

Health Canada (2022). Canadian Postsecondary Education Alcohol and Drug Use Survey, 2021-22: Public Use Microdata File user guide. Section 7.3, release guidelines.

See also

svymx() for the estimate and its standard error; svyqual() for the quality level of an estimate.

Examples

# 12% of 400 respondents, standard error 2.1 points, 38 design df
svypci(0.12, 0.021, 400, df = 38)
#>    est         lo      hi    neff
#> 1 0.12 0.08065552 0.16967 225.824
for (m in c("beta", "wilson", "logit", "wald")) {
  print(svypci(0.12, 0.021, 400, df = 38, method = m))
}
#>    est         lo      hi    neff
#> 1 0.12 0.08065552 0.16967 225.824
#>    est         lo        hi    neff
#> 1 0.12 0.08385073 0.1688613 225.824
#>    est         lo        hi    neff
#> 1 0.12 0.08355411 0.1694048 225.824
#>    est         lo        hi    neff
#> 1 0.12 0.07748772 0.1625123 225.824
# near 0 the Wald interval leaves the range; the others do not
svypci(0.01, 0.008, 400, df = 38, method = "wald")
#>    est           lo         hi     neff
#> 1 0.01 -0.006195153 0.02619515 145.8814
svypci(0.01, 0.008, 400, df = 38, method = "wilson")
#>    est          lo         hi     neff
#> 1 0.01 0.002272718 0.04287127 145.8814
try(svypci(1.2, 0.1, 400))
#> Error : svypci: `est` must be proportions, from 0 to 1.
